          DOS asks for the date and the time: press Enter two times. Click the screen first, so that your keys go to the machine. Type B: and then a program name to run it from drive B:. Drop files on a drive to copy them to its disk; drop a folder on drive C: to copy it with its subfolders (long names become DOS 8.3 names). With no disk in A:, the machine boots from C:. After you change drive C:, boot again, because DOS keeps parts of the disk in memory.

                  How to drive the machine
                  
  
                  
    
                  F5
                  Run or pause
                  
    
                  F8
                  Step one instruction
                  
    
                  Shift+F8
                  Step one clock (T-state)
                  
    
                  N or . or Space
                  Trace: next step (outside the editor)
                  
    
                  B or ,
                  Trace: back one step
                  
    
                  S
                  Trace: skip (step over a CALL, an INT or a loop)
                  
    
                  F9
                  Toggle a breakpoint on the cursor line
                  
    
                  Ctrl+Enter
                  Assemble and load
                  
    
                  Ctrl+R
                  Reset
                  
    
                  1–6
                  Board 3D, Top 2D, Runner, Die, Bus timing, Memory (outside the editor)
                  
    
                  [ / ]
                  Hide or show the program pane / the state dock
                  
    
                  F, Esc
                  Expand the machine view to the whole window, and back
                  
    
                  Top 2D
                  All the chips from above, always open. Drag: move. Wheel or +/−: zoom. Double-click a chip: fill the view. Esc: see all. Follow: the view goes to the chips that work.
                  
    
                  Board 3D mouse
                  Drag: move the view. Right-drag or Shift+drag: turn it. Wheel: zoom to the pointer. Double-click a chip: focus on it (nothing hides it); Esc leaves the focus.
                  
  
                  
  
                  Click a line number to set a breakpoint. Click the screen and type to send scan codes through the 8255 to the CPU (IRQ1). When the screen has the focus, all keys go to the machine; use the buttons to pause.
                  
  
                  To run an operating system, open Disks, load a bootable floppy image (for example your own MS-DOS 3.3 disk) into drive A:, put programs on drive B: with Add files, and press Boot from A:. The machine then runs at 4.77 MHz, and you can change the speed at any time to watch the bus traffic.
                  
  
                  Two machines: select the title (8086 ANATOMY / 80286 ANATOMY) to switch. The 80286 machine is an AT-class board at 8 MHz with an 80287, 16 MB of address space, the A20 gate, a CMOS clock and protected mode. Its samples show the new instructions, the A20 gate and a tour of protected mode.
                  
  
                  This is an original educational simulation. The board layout is inspired by the IBM PC 5150, with an 8086 in place of the 8088 and an 8087 in the coprocessor socket. The BIOS is original code; INT 21h is a tiny DOS-like subset for convenience. Instruction results were checked against 640,744 real 8086 hardware test cases.
